study.title: 2 Kings 15 - Kings, partial fidelity and the fragility of power
study.overview: The chapter presents, in parallel, two spiritual and political paths. In Judah, Azariah is also called Uzziah in the notes - does what is right before the LORD, but his obedience is incomplete: the high ones remain, and his life ends in isolation because of leprosy. After him, Jotão continues a correct administration, although he also does not remove the popular idolatry. In Israel, on the contrary, the sequence is marked by violent instability: Zechariah, Shallum, Menaem, Pecaiah and Pekas succeed by conspiracies, murders and oppression. The chapter shows both God's mercy in preserving the Davidic lineage in Judah and the judgment on Israel for persistence in the sins of Jeroboam. At the same time, Assyrian pressure appears as a sign of a deteriorating political scenario, increasing the crisis on the land.

outline.title: Azariah reigns in Judah, but their obedience is incomplete
outline.explanation: Azariah begins to reign young and rule for many years in Jerusalem. The text evaluates him positively, but highlights two limits: he does not remove the highs and the Lord hurts him with leprosy, which leads him to live separately until he dies. Jotham his son administers the people while the king remains isolated, and then succeeds his father on the throne.

outline.title: Jehu's house ends and Israel enters even more violence
outline.explanation: Zechariah reigns a short time and continues in the sins of Jeroboam. Shallum kills him, the word said to Jehu is fulfilled over his descendants to the fourth generation, and soon Shallum is also murdered by Menaem. The chapter also records Menaem's cruelty against Tifsa and its borders, showing the brutality that accompanies the power dispute.

outline.title: Menaem, Pecaías and Peca: bad government, oppression and territorial loss
outline.explanation: Menahem reigns in Samaria, and does evil in the sight of the LORD; to establish his kingdom, he pays a heavy tribute to the king of Assyria, and he shall pass the cost to the mighty men of Israel. His son Pecaiah also perseveres in evil, but is killed by Pekah, one of his captains. Afterwards, Peca reigns and the text links his days to the Assyrian invasion and the loss of cities and regions of Israel, culminating in Peka's death by swion conspiracy.

outline.title: Jotham in Judah: a right but limited king, and the threat to the kingdom
outline.explanation: Jotham will reign in Judah with a positive assessment: do what is right and even do a work connected with the house of the LORD. Even so, the highs continue to exist. At the end of his reign, the LORD began to send against Judah the pressure of Resim and Pekah, and Jotham dies, being succeeded by Ahaz.

study.context: The chapter moves between the kingdoms of Judah and Israel through cross-dates between their kings, something that the text itself uses to synchronize events. In Judah, the tradition of the city of David and the reference to the house of the LORD highlight the continuity of the Davidic dynasty and the official cult. In Israel, the text shows a chain of short and violent kings, often marked by conspiracies. The notes also associate Peca's rise to a period of greater military support and assyrian pressure on the region.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that divine assessment does not reduce the external appearance of political success. Azariah and Jotham receive a favorable testimony, but both fail to remove the highs, showing that fidelity can be real and still incomplete. In Israel, the repetition of Jeroboam's sins functions as a spiritual diagnosis: persisting in idolatry opens up room for instability, violence and judgment. The word of the LORD to Jehu, however, also shows that history is not outside of divine control; even the succession of cruel kings and the end of dynasties follow what God had announced. The chapter counters fragile human power and firm divine government, while at the same time revealing that prosperity, longevity or military victory are not automatic signs of spiritual approval. The holiness of God appears both in the correction of Judah and in the judgment on Israel.

scholarViews.insight: The notes point out that although Azariah received blessing and prosperity, he continued to allow worship in the highs; spiritual approval did not eliminate this failure in his reform.
The commentaries point out that after the end of the house of Jehu, the kingdom of Israel came into extreme confusion, with violence and unstable successions, showing a period of great disorder.
The commentary notes that the word of the LORD to Jehu was fulfilled accurately, for his descendants occupied the throne to the fourth generation.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to obey the LORD in a real way, but still incomplete, like Azariah and Jotham?
What signs does the chapter offer that idolatry and disobedience are not only in the religious field, but produce social and political effects?
How should God's faithfulness to his word, both in promise and judgment, shape our way of reading history?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine whether his obedience is partial or whole. The concrete application is to abandon modern "high" practices, alliances or habits that compete with devotion to the Lord - even when the outward life seems stable. It also invites you to resist the logic of power based on conspiracy, manipulation and violence, choosing integrity, justice and fear of God. Where there is leadership, whether in the family, in the church or at work, the text encourages to evaluate not only results but spiritual fidelity.
study.uncertainty: There is variation of names in the notes for the king of Judah, appearing as Azariah and Uzziah; the biblical text provided uses Azariah. The notes also bring some approximate historical and chronological details, but the study was limited to what was explicitly informed. On certain secondary characters, such as Argobe and Arié, the notes record ignorance of their identity; therefore, no statements were made beyond the text.
